title: One hundred twenty thousand tickets
scenario: A software company wants to label 120,000 old support tickets with a topic, using the Claude Message Batches API. A teammate wrote the first plan and ran a small test. You review the plan before the real run (exhibit).
exhibit:
(made-up example data)

PLAN v1
  job:        label 120,000 old tickets with a topic
  submit:     one Message Batch with 120,000 requests
  read:       results file, in file order, paired with tickets by line number

TEST OUTPUT (input order was ticket-1, ticket-2, ticket-3)
  line 1  custom_id: ticket-3  result.type: succeeded
  line 2  custom_id: ticket-1  result.type: succeeded
  line 3  custom_id: ticket-2  result.type: succeeded

PLAN v2: two batches of 60,000. Batch 1 has ended.
  succeeded: 59,412
  errored:      380
  canceled:       0
  expired:      208

CACHE
  every request starts with the same 2,000-token label guide,
  marked with identical cache_control blocks (5-minute cache)
  cache hit rate across batch 1: 70%

questions.prompt: Plan v1 sends 120,000 requests in one Claude batch. What should the team do?

options.text: Keep one batch. Only the 24-hour expiry limits how big it can be.
options.explanation: A Claude batch is also limited by request count and size. Whichever limit is reached first applies.

options.text: Turn on stream: true so the 120,000 results arrive in pieces.
options.explanation: stream: true is not supported in batch requests. Batch results come back as a single file.

options.text: Split it: one Claude batch holds 100,000 requests or 256 MB.
options.explanation: Right. Whichever limit is reached first applies, so plan v2 uses two batches of 60,000.

options.text: Switch to OpenAI's Batch API, whose per-batch limit is higher.
options.explanation: OpenAI allows up to 50,000 requests per batch, which is lower than Claude's 100,000.

questions.prompt: In the test output, the lines are not in input order. How should the code pair results with tickets?

options.text: By custom_id, because batch results can come back in any order.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say results may not match the input order and tell you to always use custom_id.

options.text: By line number, after sorting the tickets by id before they are sent.
options.explanation: Sorting the input does not set the output order. Results can still come back in any order.

options.text: By line number, after cutting the batches to 100 requests each.
options.explanation: Small batches have no ordering guarantee either. The order of results is not tied to batch size.

options.text: By line number, with a hand check of a few results for each batch.
options.explanation: A spot check can miss the problem. Matching by custom_id removes the risk instead of sampling it.

questions.prompt: Batch 1 ended with the counts in the exhibit. What is the right next step?

options.text: Rerun all 60,000 requests, because one failure spoils the batch.
options.explanation: The Claude docs say the failure of one request does not affect the others. 59,412 requests already succeeded.

options.text: Do nothing. Claude retries errored and expired requests by itself.
options.explanation: Claude's batch advice is to implement your own retry logic for failed requests. Nothing is retried for you.

options.text: Resubmit only the 208 expired requests, since errored ones cannot be retried.
options.explanation: Errored requests include server errors, which can be retried. Invalid requests need a fix first, then a retry.

options.text: Fix any invalid requests, then resubmit only the 588 failed ids.
options.explanation: Right. 380 errored plus 208 expired is 588. Those were not billed, and the rest are done.

questions.prompt: The cache hit rate is 70%, not 100%. What do the Claude docs say?

options.text: Expect 100%, because Anthropic guarantees every cache read in a batch.
options.explanation: The docs say cache hits in a batch are best-effort, with typical hit rates from 30% to 98%.

options.text: Hits are best-effort in a batch, so use identical blocks and the 1-hour cache.
options.explanation: Right. Requests run concurrently in any order. A batch can take longer than 5 minutes, so the docs suggest the 1-hour cache.

options.text: Keep the 5-minute cache, since every read refreshes it, and hits will reach 100%.
options.explanation: A batch can take longer than 5 minutes, and hits stay best-effort. The docs point to the 1-hour cache for batches.

options.text: Add a unique timestamp to each request so the cache spreads out its work.
options.explanation: A changing value at the start breaks the shared prefix (realm 3, chapter 4). Hits would fall, not rise.
